doc.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012

chapter: Hearing jazz and learning the camera
title: Shooting as grounding, and editing as improvisation
summary: Crohn explains how shooting suits his ADD, compares it to improvisation, and likens editing to Rodin's sculpture in the stone.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well it’s funny because when you said the cameraman said that it’s not the shooting it’s the — I thought you were going to say editing.

Well that’s true. And as any camera person will tell you if you know editing you’re already thinking about the editing when you’re shooting. But you know it’s interesting. I’m a classic ADD person. Oh God we’re going to go on a sideline here. Someone said that ADD was a useful trait before the Industrial Revolution, back when we were hunters and gatherers. Gatherers did repetitive tasks and they had to be aware in the future that if they planted their seeds and they knew their tasks in the spring would yield dividends in the fall. So they were like they were of the mentality of they could see into the future, they knew that repetitive tasks were good. The hunters had to be alert every moment, and went out in the forest, and the sound of a broken twig, or the movement, they had to be alert and ready to shoot. And I’m actually a fairly good cameraman, I think because — and also ADD people need to use their body and move around. They can’t be just in their head. Using their body grounds themselves. So when I’m with a camera I feel grounded. And I used to shoot rifles and I’m a good shot. I was very accurate as a marksman. And when you hold a camera and you move it, you feel one with the camera, you feel one with your environment, it’s like being a hunter. And one eye’s looking for what is coming up and the other eye is with the camera, and I feel more grounded, more alive, when I’m shooting as a cameraman than almost anything that I do. Because I’m using my brain and my body. I’m using my eye. I’m using all parts of my consciousness and my body and it’s where all the elements come together.
It sounds a little bit like jazz improvisation.

It is in a way and that’s a good point. I never made it as a musician but when you’re shooting you’re improvising all the time. And I also think that, as Warren would say, “Everything is everything. We’re all related.” Editing is also, you don’t create the piece, you wait for the piece to emerge and speak to you. What you’re editing. Rodin once said, “The sculpture is in the stone waiting to be revealed.” You don’t chip away and create something, it’s already in there. You just let it speak to you and you know where to chip. And out comes the sculpture that is already in there. And when I edit, if I don’t get too cerebral about it, I realize the film is in there. Now it’s footage, but somewhere the film is in there waiting to be — and you have to work really hard at clearing the debris around it to let it speak to you. And you go down many wrong paths too. You have to have a lot of

patience. I happen to be editing something now and I can’t do it on a part time thing. I have to clear away my life. I have to make sure there’s enough money that I don’t have to go out — because once you plunge into editing — it’s like writers talk about writing a book, they just plunge into writing a book. Joyce Carol Oates once said, “You don’t water the plants, you don’t dust your house, you don’t vacuum, you just write.”
